analysis.one_liner: Bans racial profiling by police and creates due-process rights for people detained by immigration agents.
analysis.headline: A bill to ban racial profiling and set immigration-detention rights, backed by 6 Democratic senators, never got a hearing or a vote in the Senate Judiciary Committee and died when the 115th Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would outlaw racial profiling by any federal, state, local, or tribal law enforcement agency, let people sue to stop it, and require agencies to collect and publish data on who they stop and search. For people caught up in immigration enforcement, it would guarantee Miranda-style warnings, access to a lawyer and a free phone call, quick filings with immigration courts, protections for parents separated from their children, and screening and release options for vulnerable detainees like pregnant women, children, and people with disabilities. It would also create an independent ombudsman to inspect detention facilities and would rescind the two January 2017 executive orders that expanded interior immigration enforcement and border enforcement.
analysis.who_benefits: Racial and ethnic minorities who are more likely to be stopped and searched, immigrants and U.S. citizens mistakenly caught in immigration raids, parents and caregivers detained away from their children, and vulnerable detainees such as pregnant women, children, LGBTQ individuals, and people with disabilities. Communities broadly gain from published data on stops and searches.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Immigrants, racial minorities, and detained parents

how_it_helps.text: Makes racial profiling illegal for all federal, state, local, and tribal law enforcement and lets individuals sue for court orders stopping it, with statistical disparities in stops treated as initial evidence [S3].

Requires all law enforcement agencies to record the race, ethnicity, national origin, gender, and religion of people they stop and search, and requires annual public reports analyzing disparities and the hit rate of searches [S3].

Gives people detained in immigration enforcement the right to counsel, a warning of the right to remain silent, a free phone call within six hours, a charging document filed with an immigration court within 48 hours, and a judge review within 72 hours [S3].

Requires prompt screening of detainees for membership in vulnerable populations, with release on recognizance or bond within 72 hours unless the government proves detention is necessary, and bars transfers or arrests that cut parents off from their children's care and custody proceedings [S3].
Creates an Immigration and Customs Enforcement Ombudsman empowered to make unannounced inspections of detention facilities, take confidential complaints from detainees, and report on compliance [S3].

Bars immigration arrests at schools, hospitals, courts, places of worship, and other sensitive locations except in emergencies, and would rescind the January 2017 executive orders directing expanded interior and border enforcement [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Federal immigration agencies and their contractors would bear the cost of tighter detention limits, ombudsman oversight, and alternatives-to-detention programs. Every federal, state, local, and tribal police agency would face new training, data-collection, and record-keeping duties, plus exposure to civil suits; private detention companies would hold fewer detainees if vulnerable populations and caregivers must be released or placed in community supervision.

drawbacks.text: The profiling ban applies to every police department in the country, not just federal agencies, and lets a statistical pattern of stops serve as initial proof of a violation, which would push many local agencies into litigation over stop patterns even where individual officers acted properly [S3].

Collecting race, ethnicity, and religion data on all stops and searches imposes a continuing administrative burden on thousands of agencies, funded by sums 'as may be necessary' appropriated by Congress [S3].

The bill would rescind Executive Orders 13768 and 13767, undoing the enforcement priorities and border-security directives the administration had set weeks earlier, which its supporters would frame as restoring restraint but which opponents would call a unilateral retreat from enforcement [S3].

Requiring release of most vulnerable-population detainees within 72 hours unless the government meets its burden of proof would shift a large share of the detained population into community supervision or release, a change opponents argued could reduce appearance rates at removal proceedings [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The core protections address documented problems: the bill's own findings cite mistaken detentions and deportations of U.S. citizens and lawful permanent residents [S3], and profiling data requirements are a proven accountability tool. The costs are real but mostly administrative, except that the release provisions for vulnerable detainees and the blanket sensitive-locations ban would significantly constrain immigration enforcement, which is exactly why it had no Republican support. The disparate-impact litigation standard is the weakest design element, inviting lawsuits against agencies whose individual officers acted reasonably.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced and referred to the Senate Judiciary Committee in March 2017, and the committee never took it up; it died when the 115th Congress ended in January 2019.

narrative.text: Sen. Robert Menendez introduced the bill on March 28, 2017, joined by Democratic Sens. Booker, Gillibrand, Harris, and Wyden [S1, S4].
The bill was read twice and referred to the Committee on the Judiciary the same day [S5].
No further action appears in the record: no hearing, markup, committee report, or floor vote [S5].
The Congress ended January 3, 2019, killing the bill automatically [S1].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Federal immigration enforcement agencies and the private detention industry kept operating under the January 2017 executive orders the bill would have rescinded, and police agencies nationwide avoided the profiling ban, data-collection mandates, and civil liability the bill would have created. Immigrants, racial minorities, and families separated by detentions did not get the protections the bill promised.

for.name: Sen. Robert Menendez
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill in the Senate.

for.name: Sens. Cory Booker, Kirsten Gillibrand, Kamala Harris, and Ron Wyden
for.role: U.S. senators from New Jersey, New York, California, and Oregon

against.name: Senate Judiciary Committee
against.role: Committee to which the bill was referred (Republican-chaired in the 115th Congress)
against.what_they_did: Referred the bill on the day of introduction and never held a hearing, markup, or vote on it during the two-year Congress.

against.name: President Donald Trump
against.what_they_did: Signed the January 2017 executive orders expanding interior and border immigration enforcement that the bill would have rescinded, and his administration's enforcement policies defined the status quo the bill sought to change.

sides.party_line_note: All six sponsors and cosponsors were Democrats and no Republican signed on, so the bill never had a path out of the Republican-run Judiciary Committee.

industries.note: The bill would require release or community-based alternatives for vulnerable detainees, caregivers, and many others, shrinking the population detention facilities hold and profit from. The bill favors community supervision programs over secure detention.

industries.industry: Federal immigration enforcement (ICE, CBP) and state/local police agencies
industries.note: Agencies would gain training, data standards, and clearer rules, but face a profiling ban, civil suits, mandatory warnings and phone access, ombudsman inspections, and a ban on arrests at sensitive locations. The industry interest in unimpeded enforcement runs against the due-process and anti-profiling interests of the people subject to it.

The bill directs DHS to contract with nongovernmental organizations for detainee screening, appearance assistance, and community supervision, and expands the market for free and low-cost legal services lists given to detainees.
